result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.simple_cycles()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find all simple cycles in the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L16498-L16595){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.simple_cycles(length_bound=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Simple cycles](/assets/graphs/simple-cycles.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="An undirected house-shaped graph: a triangle on top of a square. It has three simple cycles, each drawn in its own color: the triangle C, A, B (accent color), the outer loop C, A, B, D, E (teal), and the square C, B, D, E (violet)." width="100%"} A simple cycle is a closed path where no node appears more than once (except that the first and last node are the same). This method works for both directed and undirected graphs. For directed graphs, uses Johnson's algorithm which is efficient and finds each cycle exactly once. For undirected graphs, uses a backtracking DFS approach that finds all elementary cycles by starting from each node and exploring all paths that return to the starting node. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [length_bound]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional maximum cycle length. If specified, only cycles with at most this many nodes are returned. If `None` (default), all cycles are returned regardless of length. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A list of cycles, where each cycle is a list of node IDs forming the cycle. The start node is not repeated at the end. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Two different engines back this call. Directed graphs use Johnson's algorithm, the same one behind `get_cycles()`, at $O\!\left((V + E)(C + 1)\right)$ time. Undirected graphs fall back to a backtracking DFS that starts fresh from every node; its worst case is exponential in $V$, but a canonicalization step ensures each cycle is emitted exactly once regardless of which starting node discovered it. Cycles come back as sequences of node IDs with no repeat of the start node at the end. Pass `length_bound=` to cut off the search early when only short cycles are of interest. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Unlike `get_cycles()`, this also works on undirected graphs. A directed graph with a 2-cycle and a 3-cycle produces exactly two simple cycles: ::: {#17ec064a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), # closes A -> B -> C -> A ("B", "A"), # closes A -> B -> A ] ) ) len(graph.simple_cycles()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: An undirected triangle has exactly one cycle, since each direction around the loop is the same cycle: ::: {#808d30ce .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) len(graph.simple_cycles()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: `length_bound=` excludes any cycle longer than the given size -- here, the 4-cycle is filtered out, leaving only the 2-cycle: ::: {#64b92f79 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("B", "A"), # 2-cycle ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "A"), # 4-cycle ] ) ) graph.simple_cycles(length_bound=3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [[1, 2]] ``` ::: :::
